title: How to Fix the #N/A Error in Excel
dek: The #N/A error means a lookup could not find what it was searching for — VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP, or MATCH came up empty. The fix is to check the lookup value for typos, spaces, and type mismatches, or handle it cleanly with IFNA. Here is how.

intent.primaryKeyword: how to fix na error in excel

seo.metaTitle: How to Fix the #N/A Error in Excel
seo.metaDescription: The #N/A error means a lookup found no match. Learn what causes it in VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP, how to fix the data, and how to handle it cleanly with IFNA.

sources.label: Microsoft Support — How to correct a #N/A error

richText: #N/A stands for "not available", and it means a lookup could not find what you asked for. It shows up most often with VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP, MATCH, and INDEX MATCH — the function searched, found no match, and reported back honestly. The good news: the cause is almost always small and easy to fix.

items: The lookup value genuinely is not in the list you are searching.
A trailing or leading space makes "North " and "North" look different to Excel.
A number is stored as text in one place and as a real number in the other, so they never match.
VLOOKUP is missing its final FALSE, so it does an approximate match on unsorted data.
A small typo in the lookup value or the search range.

body.text: Step 1: Confirm the value really exists

richText: First, check that what you are searching for is actually in the lookup column. Use a quick test next to your data —
returns how many times the value in D1 appears. If it returns 0, the value is not there (or not there in the form you typed it).

items: Strip stray spaces with TRIM, like =TRIM(D1), or clean the whole column with Find & Replace.
Make the types match: if the list holds real numbers, the lookup value must be a number too, not text. Data > Text to Columns > Finish quickly converts text-numbers.
For VLOOKUP, add FALSE as the last argument to force an exact match: =VLOOKUP(D1, A2:B100, 2, FALSE).

body.richText: Hidden spaces are the number-one cause. If "North" clearly exists but still returns #N/A, try =VLOOKUP(TRIM(D1), ...) or clean the source column — the culprit is usually a space you cannot see.

body.text: Step 3: Handle it cleanly with IFNA

richText: Sometimes a #N/A is expected — the value simply is not there yet. Instead of an ugly error, show a friendly message with IFNA, which catches only #N/A and leaves other errors visible:
IFNA is better than IFERROR here because it hides only the not-found case, so a real mistake elsewhere still shows up. This error is most common with the lookup family —
. XLOOKUP even has a built-in not-found argument, so it can skip IFNA entirely.

items.question: Why does my VLOOKUP return #N/A when the value is clearly there?
items.answerRichText: Almost always a hidden space or a type mismatch. The value may have a trailing space, or it is stored as text in one place and as a number in the other. Wrap the lookup value in TRIM and make sure both sides are the same data type.

items.question: What is the difference between IFNA and IFERROR?
items.answerRichText: IFNA catches only the #N/A error, while IFERROR catches every error type. Use IFNA for lookups so that a genuine problem elsewhere — like a #REF! or #VALUE! — still shows up instead of being hidden.

items.question: How do I remove #N/A from a whole column?
items.answerRichText: Wrap each lookup in IFNA to replace #N/A with a blank or a message, like =IFNA(VLOOKUP(...), ""). Fix the underlying data where you can, and use IFNA only to handle the cases that are genuinely expected to be missing.
